scope: Code and documentation style only. Portable across projects. Contains no project-specific architecture.
precedence: If this file disagrees with surrounding code, match the surrounding code and flag the conflict.

hard_rules: ASCII characters only. No em dashes, en dashes, arrows, degree signs, multiplication signs, ellipsis characters, curly quotes, or accented letters. Write -> not an arrow character, write 1x1 not a multiplication sign, write 90 degrees or 90deg not a degree symbol.
Canadian English spelling. colour, centre, normalise, behaviour, licence (noun), grey, metre, catalogue, travelled.
No trailing period at the end of a comment. This applies to the last sentence only; periods between sentences inside a multi-sentence comment are correct and expected.
No non-restrictive modifier words. Cut anything that softens or inflates without adding information.

banned_words.note: These are the non-restrictive modifiers to avoid. The list is illustrative, not exhaustive.
banned_words.rationale: They either soften a claim that should stand on its own or pad a sentence that is already clear.

terminology.preference: Older, traditional technical terms over their newer replacements. This is a deliberate style choice, not an oversight.

examples.master: not main, for a primary branch or primary/replica relationship
examples.slave: not replica or secondary, where the codebase already uses master

terminology.scope: Applies to comments, variable and function names, and documentation. Match whatever term the surrounding codebase already uses; do not silently swap in a newer synonym while editing nearby code.

voice.register: Casual and plain-spoken, like explaining to a colleague at the next desk. Lowercase-leaning starts are fine and normal.
voice.technical_terms: Use precise terms when they keep the comment shorter. Do not simplify 'quaternion' into 'rotation thing'.
voice.contractions: Fine and preferred. do not, does not, cannot as words is too stiff for this voice.
voice.person: First person plural for what the code does ('we strip the sheen', 'so we block'). Second person for consequences to the reader ('you get no geometry').

content.principle: Explain WHY, not WHAT. The code says what it does.
write_comments_for: A non-obvious cause, especially one discovered by debugging
A past bug this code prevents, with enough detail that nobody reverts it
An external library's surprising behaviour or units
A deliberate trade-off and what was given up
An invariant that looks like dead code and invites deletion
do_not_write: TODO without context on what and why
content.why_good: Names the external behaviour, the unit, the conversion, and the bug it caused. Nobody will 'clean up' the multiplication.
content.why_bad: Restates the code, explains nothing, and ends with a period.

formatting.wrap_width: Wrap comment lines at about 80 characters. Median in this codebase is 77, p90 is 80.
formatting.block_comments: Use // on every line. Do not use /* */ in JavaScript.
formatting.section_rules: Major sections get a banner: a line of 75 dashes after '// ', then a lowercase title line, then another rule if it opens a large region. Smaller sections use a single trailing-dash line: '// ---- the proxy endpoint itself ----------------------------------------------'
formatting.inline_comments: Align trailing comments in a run of related declarations so the // characters line up. Keep them to one short clause.
formatting.inline_example:
let currentModel = null;   // the centred/scaled group sitting in the pivot
let currentName = 'model'; // name of the loaded model, used for the gif filename
let baseDistance = 5;      // the camera Z that framed the model at zoom 1

javascript.quotes: Single quotes for strings. Double quotes only inside JSON or when the string contains an apostrophe. Template literals for interpolation.
javascript.declarations: const by default, let when reassigned, never var.
javascript.functions: Named function declarations for anything called from more than one place or hoisted. Arrow functions for callbacks, handlers, and one-liners.

naming.constants: SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for true module-level constants and tuning values
naming.private_scratch: leading underscore for module-level reused scratch objects and stashed state, e.g. _alphaCanvas, _matteSaved
naming.style: Descriptive over short. loadGeneration not gen, classifyTextureAlpha not checkAlpha.

javascript.tuning_values: Pull magic numbers out into named constants at the top of their section, with an inline comment giving the unit or reason.
javascript.error_handling: try/catch around anything touching untrusted input, external libraries, or canvas. Fail to a safe default rather than throwing. Comment the fallback with why it is safe.

css.location: In a <style> block in the HTML, not a separate file, unless the project already splits them.
css.custom_properties: Define the palette and fonts as CSS variables in :root and reference them everywhere. Never hardcode a repeated colour.
css.section_comments: Same banner style as JavaScript, using /* ---- lowercase title ------ */
css.responsive: One breakpoint block at the end rather than scattered media queries.
css.naming: Lowercase with hyphens for classes, camelCase for ids that JavaScript reaches for.

html.structure: Semantic where it matters, but do not add wrappers with no purpose.
html.ids: Every id referenced from JavaScript must exist exactly once. Verify before shipping.

general: No build step unless the project already has one. Ask before introducing a bundler.
Pin external dependencies to exact versions.
Prefer doing untrusted work client-side when a server alternative would add attack surface.

readme.voice: Same casual register as comments, slightly more complete sentences. Written as the project owner talking, not as marketing copy.
readme.sentence_case: Headings in sentence case, not Title Case.
readme.formatting: Light. Bold for the occasional key term. Avoid heavy nesting, decorative separators, and emoji.
readme.trailing_periods: Prose sentences in prose paragraphs keep their periods. Bullet list items do NOT get a trailing period.
readme.tables: Good for env vars and options. Lowercase the Purpose column entries and skip trailing periods.
readme.code_blocks: Always tag the language. Include copy-pasteable commands, not descriptions of commands.
readme.honesty: State limits plainly in a notes section. A known limitation written down is worth more than an unqualified claim.

commit_messages.subject: Imperative mood, lowercase after any prefix, no trailing period, under 72 characters.
commit_messages.body: Explain why, and name the symptom if it is a fix. Wrap at 72.
commit_messages.example:
fix gif delay unit so the fps control works

gifenc's writeFrame takes milliseconds and stores round(ms/10) as
centiseconds. we were passing centiseconds, so every delay collapsed to
0-1cs and browsers clamped it to ~100ms. that made the fps dial appear
to do nothing and duration track only frame count.

communication.note: How to report work back, not how to write code.
rules: Lead with what changed and whether it worked. Do not open with a preamble.
State the root cause when fixing a bug. 'Fixed the flicker' is less useful than naming the sorting behaviour that caused it.
Report what was verified and what could not be. Never imply a visual result was confirmed when only syntax was checked.
Flag assumptions and residual risks without being asked.
Say when something is best-effort rather than solid.
Do not pad with restatements of the request.

verification.usage: Run from the project root before shipping. Adjust the FILES list per project.
verification.note: The US-spelling and banned-word patterns are a starting point, not exhaustive. They catch the common cases.

quick_checklist: No trailing period on the final sentence of a comment
Older term used over its newer replacement (whitelist, master, etc), matching what the codebase already uses
Single quotes, 2-space indent, const by default
Every JavaScript-referenced id exists in the HTML
README bullets have no trailing periods
Limits and residual risks written down
